title: Effects of semaglutide on cardiac structure and function in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction and obesity: a pre-specified cardiac magnetic resonance substudy of the CAMEO-SEMA trial
desc: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists improve symptoms in patients with obesity and heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF). We recently demonstrated that semaglutide reduces exertional pulmonary artery wedge pressure (PAWP) in obesity-related HFpEF, but potential effects of semaglutide on cardiac structure and function that may underlie these hemodynamic improvements remain unclear. In this prespecified cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) substudy of the randomized CAMEO-SEMA trial, 49 participants (33 semaglutide, 16 placebo, 28 female) underwent CMR at baseline and 52 weeks, within 1 day of invasive exercise hemodynamic assessment. The prespecified primary CMR endpoint was change in left atrial (LA) reservoir strain; other prespecified CMR endpoints included LV filling dynamics, which were assessed by early filling rate indexed to end-diastolic volume (eFR/EDV). Compared with placebo, semaglutide improved LA reservoir strain (+5.7% [95% CI, +0.3 to +9.7]; P=0.037) and eFR/EDV (+0.64 s−1 [95% CI, +0.42 to +1.00]; P<0.0001). Improvements in LA reservoir strain and LV filling dynamics were associated with reductions in exercise PAWP (r=−0.46, P<0.001 and r=−0.65, P<0.0001, respectively). With respect to other prespecified CMR endpoints, semaglutide reduced LV mass, restored more physiologic LV geometry, and improved right ventricular function and biventricular myocardial mechanics. The results of this CMR substudy indicate that in patients with obesity-related HFpEF, semaglutide improves LA function and LV diastolic filling dynamics, identifying improvements in myocardial function that may contribute to semaglutide’s improvement of hemodynamics. ClinicalTrials.gov number: NCT05371496.

title: Large language models are unstable as autonomous medical evaluators across clinical tasks.
source: PubMed · Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
desc: [Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA] Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as automated evaluators of medical text ("LLM-as-judge"). We tested whether LLM-evaluator performance validated on one medical task against a human reference standard remains stable on a structurally different task. We evaluated 10 LLMs (3 locally served open-source and 7 API models: Claude, GPT, DeepSeek) as autonomous judges on 3 tasks with human reference labels: LiveQA-Med answer quality (n = 300), PubMedQA research appraisal (n = 300), and Emergency Severity Index (ESI) triage on MIMIC-IV-Ext (n = 256). Each case was scored 3 times per model at temperature zero (25 680 judgments). Analyses used cluster-bootstrap confidence intervals, quadratic-weighted Cohen's κ, and false-discovery-rate correction. Evaluator performance was unstable across tasks: no model ranked in the top 3 on all 3 tasks, and every model shifted by 3 or more rank positions between at least one pair of tasks. In the highest-stakes task, ESI level 1 (Resuscitation) cases were under-triaged in 89.1% of evaluations, in all 10 models (range 70.2%-96.9%). Best triage agreement only reached the human inter-rater range (Claude Opus quadratic-weighted κ = 0.60 [0.54, 0.66]). Locally served 7-27B models (no per-query charge) occupied the Pareto frontier on the text tasks but only its low-concordance end on triage. LLM-evaluator performance is unstable between medical tasks that differ in cognitive structure; performance validated on one task should not be assumed to transfer to another. Task-specific validation against human reference labels is required before deployment, and emergency triage demands human oversight at the highest-acuity tier.

title: Artificial intelligence in Saudi otolaryngology research: a scoping review of the current landscape, gaps, and future directions.
desc: [Frontiers in surgery] Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in otolaryngology, but the extent and focus of AI research in Saudi Arabia remain unclear. This scoping review mapped the available evidence and identified key research themes and knowledge gaps. A scoping review was conducted following the PRISMA-ScR guidelines. PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, Google Scholar, and the Saudi Medical Journal archive were searched for studies published between January 2019 and April 2026. Eligible studies investigated AI applications or clinician perspectives within Saudi otolaryngology. The evidence was mapped across major otolaryngology domains, including cochlear implantation and hearing, rhinology and skull base surgery, facial plastic surgery, laryngology and voice, head and neck oncology, surgical and other ENT-related interventions for obstructive sleep apnoea, AI education and implementation, and AI-assisted patient education. The searches identified 2,925 database records, four records from other sources and seven records from an updated search and expert suggestions; thirteen studies met the inclusion criteria. The evidence covered AI awareness and education, large language model (LLM)-based patient education, cochlear implantation, rhinology and skull base surgery, facial plastic surgery, laryngology and voice, and head and neck oncology; no eligible study addressed surgical or other ENT-related interventions for obstructive sleep apnoea. Clinicians were generally positive about AI, while clinical studies showed promising performance of AI models. LLM chatbots generally gave accurate postoperative advice, although, when validated tools were used, their responses were harder to read and less actionable than patient-education standards recommend. However, limited AI education, small or non-Saudi datasets, limited external validation, and implementation barriers remained important challenges. AI research in Saudi otolaryngology remains limited but is expanding across several clinical domains. Future research should prioritise Saudi-specific datasets, multicentre clinical validation, structured AI education, rigorous bilingual (Arabic and English) evaluation of LLM-generated patient information, and safe integration of AI into clinical practice in line with Saudi Vision 2030.

title: Methodological Adherence, Reporting Completeness, and Risk of Bias in AI-Assisted Systematic Reviews: A Matched Meta-Research Study
desc: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to accelerate systematic reviews that inform clinical practice and policy. However, evidence on the methodological adherence, reporting completeness, and risk of bias of completed AI-assisted reviews is limited. Objective: To compare methodological adherence, reporting completeness, and risk of bias between published systematic reviews with reported AI assistance and matched reviews with no reported AI use, and to assess AI-use transparency. Methods: We conducted a matched-cohort meta-research study of English-language, peer-reviewed health systematic reviews. AI-assisted reviews published during 2023--2025 were matched 1:2 to reviews with no reported AI use using individualized MEDLINE searches targeting publication timing, clinical domain, review type, and meta-analysis status. When more than two eligible comparators were available, two were randomly selected. AI assistance was defined as reported use during searching, screening, data extraction, risk-of-bias assessment, evidence synthesis, or substantive drafting. Full texts and supplementary materials were examined to classify reported AI use. The primary outcome was a prespecified modified 13-item AMSTAR-2 methodological-adherence score (range 0 -- 13; noninferiority margin &-1 point). Secondary outcomes included PRISMA 2020 reporting completeness and ROBIS risk of bias; AI-use transparency was assessed descriptively. Adapted 13-item AMSTAR-2 confidence categories were summarized descriptively, while critical- and noncritical-domain adherence was examined in exploratory adjusted analyses. Multivariable regression models adjusted for journal impact tier, funding reporting, formal review-group affiliation, review-team size, and review-question type, using cluster-robust standard errors by matched set. Sensitivity analyses included matched-set fixed-effects models. The study was registered on the Open Science Framework (DOI: 10.17605/OSF.IO/Q5JRW). Results: The cohort included 231 systematic reviews: 77 AI-assisted and 154 with no reported AI use. Mean 13-item AMSTAR-2 scores were 7.58 and 9.63, respectively. In multivariable-adjusted analyses, AI-assisted reviews scored 1.64 points lower (95% CI &-2.37 to &- 0.91); noninferiority was not demonstrated. PRISMA adherence was estimated to be 4.7 percentage points lower among AI-assisted reviews in primary adjusted analyses (95% CI &-8.9 to &-0.6) and 6.4 points lower in matched-set fixed-effects

Predictive Analytics and Workflow Automation to Reduce Administrative Burden and Clinician Burnout in United States Clinical Settings: A Systematic Review.
source: PubMed · Advances in health information science and practice
desc: [Advances in health information science and practice] Electronic health record (EHR)-related administrative burden remains a frequently cited contributor to clinician burnout in the United States. Although digital systems were implemented to improve quality, safety, and care coordination, expanded documentation requirements, inbox messaging, and regulatory reporting have increased clerical workload. Traditional interruptive clinical decision support tools may further increase cognitive demands through alert fatigue and workflow disruption. Health systems have increasingly adopted predictive analytics and workflow-integrated automation, including ambient artificial intelligence (AI) documentation, inbox prioritization, and audit log-based workflow monitoring. However, their effects on operational efficiency and clinician well-being remain uncertain. This review examined clinician-facing interventions in US clinical settings and their impact on documentation workload, operational efficiency, and burnout-related outcomes. A systematic review guided by Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses was conducted using PubMed, CINAHL, and Embase. The search included English-language studies published between January 1, 2019, and December 31, 2025, with an updated search capturing eligible early online publications through 2026. Eligible studies evaluated clinician-facing predictive analytics or workflow automation in US clinical settings and reported measurable outcomes, including documentation time, after-hours EHR use, alert burden, cognitive task load, productivity, or validated burnout measures. Findings were synthesized narratively because interventions and outcome measures varied. Of 520 records identified, 173 unique records were screened; 24 (13.9%) underwent full-text review, and 7 of 24 (29.2%) met inclusion criteria. Ambient AI documentation platforms were associated with approximately 10%-30% reductions in documentation time, although findings on after-hours EHR activity varied. Several multisite implementations reported improvements in validated burnout measures and cognitive task load. AI-driven inbox prioritization reduced message review time, while audit log-based clinical decision support monitoring identified changes in EHR activity patterns following intervention. Evidence quality varied, and follow-up periods were generally short. The measure that matters: What medicine asks of artificial intelligence.
desc: [Artificial intelligence in medicine] Medical artificial intelligence (AI) is advancing at unprecedented speed, yet the dominant question in the field, how well does a model perform, diverges from what clinicians ask of it in practice. Did it help someone survive? In this Position Paper, we argue that a misalignment exists between how the AI community evaluates success and how clinicians define value. Even the strongest randomized trials of clinical large language models measure subspecialist preference rather than patient survival, and in a 2024 scoping review of 86 randomized trials of AI in clinical practice, only 17% had a primary endpoint related to patient symptoms or behavior. Surveys of clinicians point to a further dimension that no benchmark captures, the erosion of human connection between clinician and patient. We propose a life-centered evaluation framework built on five principles, namely outcome primacy, dynamic evaluation, clinician co-design, relational outcomes, and transparent failure publication. The measure that ultimately matters is whether a system keeps a patient out of the intensive care unit, prevents a resuscitation, or spares a family a preventable loss.

Evaluating Frontline Health Workers' Responses to Patient Inquiries With and Without Large Language Model Support in Nigeria: Observational Study.
source: PubMed · Journal of medical Internet research
desc: [Journal of medical Internet research] Frontline health workers in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) often face barriers that compromise care quality, including limited training, high patient loads, inadequate access to updated clinical guidance, and resource constraints. Working in underserved settings further exacerbates challenges to providing accurate, complete, and empathetic responses. Addressing these gaps requires innovative tools to support FLWs in real time. This study aims to evaluate the effectiveness of ChatGPT-3.5 (OpenAI) in enhancing the quality of FLWs' responses to health inquiries in Lagos, Nigeria. In this observational study, 36 licensed frontline health workers (doctors, nurses, and community health workers) practicing general or primary care in Lagos, Nigeria, generated responses to 15 patient-generated health questions covering maternal and neonatal health, family planning, and sexually transmitted infections. Each FLW produced responses using their own knowledge and available resources (human-only) and with ChatGPT-3.5 assistance (GPT-aided). A panel of 4 clinicians evaluated responses using a 5-point Likert scale for accuracy, empathy, contextualization, completeness, safety, and overall preference. In addition, 8 nonclinician health seekers assessed a subset of responses across 3 themes: Caring, Trust, and Ease of Understanding. Across 1080 responses from 36 frontline health workers, GPT-aided responses significantly outperformed human-only responses on all clinician-rated metrics (P<.001), with the largest gains observed in completeness, empathy, and overall preference, particularly among community health extension workers (CHEWs). Nonclinician evaluators also favored GPT-aided responses across all themes, with a strong preference for trust. This study provides empirical evidence that a large language model (ChatGPT-3.5) enhances the completeness, empathy, and perceived trust of responses by frontline health workers in Lagos, Nigeria. These findings underscore the potential of integrating ChatGPT-3.5 to strengthen health care delivery in resource-limited settings, highlighting the necessity for capacity building and further investigation into its safe, equitable, and effective implementation.

Predicting acute radiation dermatitis in breast cancer patients using artificial intelligence: a systematic review.
source: PubMed · Quantitative imaging in medicine and surgery
desc: [Quantitative imaging in medicine and surgery] Acute radiation dermatitis (ARD) is a common toxicity of breast cancer radiotherapy that affects quality of life. Artificial intelligence (AI)-based models have been increasingly developed to predict ARD, but their methodological quality and clinical readiness remain unclear. This study aimed to systematically evaluate AI-based prediction models for ARD. A systematic search of PubMed, Embase (Ovid), Web of Science, and MEDLINE (Ovid) was conducted for studies published up to December 1, 2025. Studies were eligible if they developed and/or validated AI-based models for predicting ARD in patients with breast cancer receiving radiotherapy. Data were extracted using the CHARMS framework. Model quality, applicability, and risk of bias were assessed using the Prediction Model Risk of Bias Assessment Tool plus Artificial Intelligence (PROBAST + AI) tool. Given the substantial heterogeneity among studies, a qualitative synthesis was performed. Nineteen studies involving 8,506 patients were included, with sample sizes ranging from 20 to 2,058. Most studies were single-center (16/19), and only three were multicenter. Validation area under the curve (AUC) values ranged from 0.66 to 0.99. The models incorporated clinical, dosimetric, radiomics, and/or dosiomics features, with 5-154 predictors in the final models. Calibration and decision curve analysis were rarely reported, and no study performed external validation. Most studies had a high or unclear risk of bias according to PROBAST + AI, mainly related to small sample sizes, incomplete reporting, and lack of external validation. Although current AI-based models for predicting ARD in breast cancer radiotherapy demonstrate promising discriminatory performance, their methodological limitations and lack of external validation limit their readiness for routine clinical implementation. Future studies with more rigorous designs, standardized outcome assessment, transparent reporting, and independent external validation are required to facilitate clinical translation.

title: Role of smartphone-based digital adherence support for glaucoma medication therapy.
source: PubMed · Canadian journal of ophthalmology. Journal canadien d'ophtalmologie
desc: [Canadian journal of ophthalmology. Journal canadien d'ophtalmologie] Sustained adherence to intraocular pressure-lowering medications is essential for preventing progressive visual loss in patients with glaucoma on pharmacotherapy. However, adherence remains suboptimal across patient populations as the result of cognitive, behavioural, physical, and socioeconomic barriers. Recent advances in digital health have introduced smartphone-based adherence supports intended to reinforce glaucoma medication routines, improve treatment organization, and support self-management. This narrative review synthesises evidence examining smartphone-based reminder applications and related digital adherence supports in glaucoma care, with attention to usability, patient experience, behavioural determinants, and clinical feasibility. Preliminary studies have reported improvements in short-term self-reported adherence and glaucoma-specific quality of life, particularly among patients with low baseline adherence. However, reminder-based interventions may provide only temporary benefit if they do not address broader structural, behavioural, and situational barriers to adherence. Current evidence remains limited by short follow-up durations, reliance on self-reported adherence measures, and limited evaluation of long-term clinical outcomes such as intraocular pressure stability and visual field preservation. Digital adherence tools may therefore be most effective when integrated alongside broader behavioural and relationship-based support strategies, including patient education, clinician communication, and caregiver involvement. Emerging technologies such as automated messaging systems and artificial intelligence-assisted tools may represent future directions for adherence support, although evidence in glaucoma remains limited. Further research is required to establish personalised, durable, and equitable adherence support frameworks in glaucoma care.

title: Deep learning-based CT lesion analysis and radiological burden stratification in clinically diagnosed ventilator-associated pneumonia.
desc: [Frontiers in medicine] Ventilator associated pneumonia (VAP) is a major complication in the intensive care unit (ICU) and requires objective computed tomography (CT) evaluation. Therefore, this article conducted a retrospective research analysis and developed a multimodal deep learning framework. Firstly, this retrospective study included 512 patients clinically diagnosed with VAP, and then utilized a developed multimodal deep learning framework for voxel-level lesion segmentation, multi-label radiological discovery classification, and radiological burden grading. This framework integrates the anatomical priors of TotalSegmenter, a three-dimensional (3D) Swin UNETR multitasking network, and cross attention fusion of CT features and ventilation parameters. Ultimately, the study showed that the Dice score for internal validation was 0.847, the macroscopic mean area (AUC) under the subject's working characteristic curve was 0.919, and the weighted kappa was 0.826. External validation showed a Dice score of 0.821, with no significant difference between scanner manufacturers. After adjusting for clinical covariates, including acute physiology and chronic health assessment II (APACHE II) scores, there was still a significant correlation between radiation load level and 28 day mortality (hazard ratio [HR] = 2.34, P < 0.001), supporting its potential prognostic relevance.

title: Upper airway morphometry in acute neck infections: Clinical associations and deep learning-based segmentation.
desc: [European journal of radiology] Upper airway (UA) compromise is a significant and potentially life-threatening complication of acute neck infection (ANI), but objective, quantitative imaging features are lacking. This study aimed to evaluate the association between UA morphometry in emergency neck MRI and disease severity in ANI, and to develop and evaluate a deep learning (DL)-based model for automatic UA segmentation in ANI patients. A total of 322 patients were included. UA lumen was manually segmented, and prespecified morphometric features were extracted. UA morphometry was correlated with clinical outcomes. Interobserver agreement for all extracted features was evaluated with the Intraclass Correlation Coefficient (ICC). An nnU-Net model was trained on manually segmented data, and its performance was evaluated using the Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) and feature-specific ICCs. ICU admission occurred in 33/322 patients (10.2 %) and prolonged stay (>5 days) in 47/319 (14.7 %). Minimum cross-sectional area, compactness, maximum midline shift, and length of airway narrowing were associated with ICU admission (false-discovery-rate q ≤ 0.008) but not with prolonged stay, and did not significantly improve an established clinical model (AUC 0.80 to 0.84, DeLong p = 0.07 to 0.12). Interobserver agreement was moderate-to-excellent. The nnU-Net reached a median DSC of 0.920 with ICCs of 0.853 to 0.973 and reproduced the ICU associations. Quantitative UA morphometry in ANI is reproducible. A narrow caliber, a long narrowed segment, and lateral displacement of the airway are associated with ICU admission, without demonstrated incremental value over established predictors in the prespecified comparison. nnU-Net segmentation reproduces the features and their univariable associations.

title: Generative artificial intelligence in breast imaging.
source: PubMed · Journal of medical imaging (Bellingham, Wash.)
desc: [Journal of medical imaging (Bellingham, Wash.)] We aim to present a consolidated overview of current achievements in generative artificial intelligence (AI) in breast imaging, identify prevalent technical and clinical challenges alongside the strategies employed to overcome them, and highlight critical directions for future investigation. A comprehensive literature search has been conducted in PubMed, MEDLINE, and Embase for peer-reviewed journal publications since 2020, with the final search performed in October 2025. The review focuses on common methodologies, performance metrics, and strategies used to address existing hurdles in breast imaging. The 120 included papers were categorized by application, ranging from technical and/or clinical tasks-image synthesis (including 24 data augmentation, 10 enhancement, 20 image-to-image translation, and 2 secure data sharing papers), 12 segmentation, 5 reconstruction, and 16 classification papers-as well as 17 papers in radiology workflow improvement, 13 papers in the development of medical education materials, and 7 papers on solving beyond our defined tasks (six papers were assigned more than one application). Papers in each category showed their own potential to solve the task of interests. However, we identified six common challenges and concerns, such as lack of standardized evaluation for synthetic outputs, across papers that the future research should be focused on. Recent works across the field of generative AI in breast imaging have demonstrated transformative potential in clinical workflows. However, there still exists technical and ethical gaps to be addressed for safe, reliable, and equitable deployment of the generative AI models to routine medical practice.

title: Multimodal imaging and artificial intelligence for bone tumor diagnosis: Comparative performance and emerging technologies.
desc: [Journal of bone oncology] Multimodal imaging is central to the diagnosis, staging, and management of bone tumors. Radiography and computed tomography remain essential for initial assessment and cortical evaluation, magnetic resonance imaging provides superior soft tissue contrast and local staging accuracy, and positron emission tomography enhances detection of metastatic disease and treatment response. No single technique suffices across clinical scenarios. Advances in artificial intelligence and radiomics offer avenues to augment this framework, with demonstrated potential in lesion classification, segmentation, prognostication, and response prediction. This review advances a specific argument rather than surveying available technologies: that the principal constraint on artificial intelligence in musculoskeletal oncology is the stability of the reference standard rather than algorithmic capability. Ground truth in bone tumors is unstable on four grounds. Core needle biopsy samples a limited volume and may miss the highest-grade component: agreement between biopsy and resection grade in central chondrosarcoma falls from a weighted kappa of 0.63 in long bones to 0.12 in the pelvis. Expert interpretation is itself inconsistent, with interobserver kappa for grading cartilaginous tumors of 0.44 among musculoskeletal pathologists and 0.35 among radiologists. Molecular criteria have redefined entities within the past decade, so older datasets contain classes that no longer exist as defined. And histological classification does not reliably predict clinical behavior. Consequently, measurable accuracy has a ceiling set by the reference standard rather than the algorithm, and apparent failure on external validation may reflect label divergence between institutions rather than model deficiency. Evidence is graded throughout, and clinical readiness distinguished from technical performance. No system for primary bone tumor characterization has regulatory clearance in the United States or Europe, and formal appraisal of this literature confirms low methodological compliance and infrequent external validation. Progress will depend on multicenter validation and protocol harmonization, and, distinctively for this field, on composite reference standards, outcome-based endpoints, and explicit uncertainty modelling, since ground-truth instability can be mitigated but not eliminated.

title: Artificial intelligence in esophageal cancer radiotherapy: a literature review.
desc: [Journal of thoracic disease] Radiotherapy is a key component in the management of esophageal cancer (EC). Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative tool for optimizing radiotherapy workflows. Numerous AI-based tools are being developed to improve efficiency and facilitate the personalization of radiation oncology. This study aimed to provide an up-to-date review of the literature on recent advances in AI applications across the EC radiotherapy workflow. The PubMed, Embase, and Web of Science databases were searched to retrieve original English-language articles published from January 1, 2020 to May 26, 2026. The following search terms were used: "Esophageal neoplasms", "esophageal cancer", "oesophageal cancer" AND "artificial intelligence", "AI" AND "radiation oncology", "radiotherapy", "radiation", "chemoradiotherapy". The included studies covered different steps in the radiotherapy workflow; that is, initial treatment decision-making, treatment planning and preparation, treatment delivery, and post-treatment follow-up. A total of 105 studies covering the different stages of the radiotherapy workflow were included in the review. Most studies focused on initial treatment decision-making, primarily benefit-risk stratification through predictive modeling of treatment outcomes and treatment-related toxicities, followed by treatment planning and preparation, particularly automated segmentation and treatment planning. Conversely, few studies investigated AI applications in treatment plan approval and quality assurance, or treatment delivery. Notably, most of the included studies were retrospective, with substantial heterogeneity in study designs, methodologies, and reporting. AI demonstrates substantial potential to facilitate clinical decision-making while improving the efficiency and accuracy of radiotherapy workflows. Future research should prioritize multicenter prospective studies, standardized methodological and reporting frameworks, and explainable AI (XAI) to improve the reliability, transparency, and clinical translation of AI models.

title: Metabolic reprogramming of myeloid‑derived suppressor cells in colorectal cancer: Mechanistic insights and immunometabolic targeted rehabilitation (Review).
desc: [Molecular medicine reports] Metabolic reprogramming of myeloid‑derived suppressor cells (MDSCs) plays a role in immunotherapy resistance in colorectal cancer (CRC). This metabolic reprogramming appears to be coordinated by oncogenic mutations (such as adenomatous polyposis coli, KRAS and TP53) through a proposed self‑reinforcing 'mutation‑metabolism‑suppression' axis. In the present review, four core metabolic pillars sustaining MDSC pathogenicity and the epimetabolic regulation that durably locks them into a suppressive state were examined. Furthermore, two emerging dimensions were highlighted: The spatial metabolic antagonism through which MDSCs may construct a metabolically hostile zone to limit the functional activity of tertiary lymphoid structures, and the remote manipulation of MDSC function by gut and intratumoral microbiota‑derived metabolites. To transcend the limitations of non‑specific myeloid depletion, immunometabolic rehabilitation is proposed as a potentially transformative framework targeting intrinsic metabolic vulnerabilities to functionally reprogram MDSCs from an immunosuppressive to a homeostatic or immunostimulatory phenotype. By integrating emerging spatial omics for precise target validation, artificial intelligence‑guided rational drug design and microbiome modulation, this paradigm provides a strategic roadmap for next‑generation precision immunotherapy, aiming to achieve durable responses across both microsatellite stable and microsatellite instability‑high CRC.

title: Lead Optimization in Drug Discovery: Integrating Advanced Computational Approaches for Enhanced Drug Design.
desc: [Current computer-aided drug design] The process of drug discovery is complex, lengthy, and expensive; it can take more than a decade to succeed and demands significant investments of financial resources. Despite these efforts, drug candidates still experience high failure rates during clinical trials. Computeraided Drug Design (CADD) has emerged as a powerful tool to overcome these obstacles in pharmaceutical research. CADD is used for drug development, such as target identification, lead discovery, optimisation, ADMET, and drug repurposing. CADD reduces the time and cost of drug discovery. Computational chemistry, bioinformatics, and structural biology are incorporated to predict drug-target interactions. The two major methodologies used to identify and optimise potential drug candidates are Structure-Based Drug Design (SBDD) and Ligand-Based Drug Design (LBDD). Molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulations, Quantitative Structure- Activity Relationship (QSAR) modelling, pharmacophore modelling, and virtual screening are the techniques that allow efficient prediction of binding affinity, molecular behaviour, and biological activity. The recent advent of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has also enhanced CADD tools by screening large datasets, predicting pharmacokinetic properties, and designing new molecules. These developments have boosted the efficiency, accuracy, and success rate of drug discovery. (CADD) reduces time costs, as do the physical and technological capabilities of the field of computational technologies. The integration of AI continues to grow, and CADD is bound to assume a more crucial role in designing safer and more efficient therapeutic agents in the future. In this review, we will discuss the general concepts of CADD, the methodologies of CADD, and CADD in drug discovery.

title: AI-Anxiety, Hope, and Techno-Subjunctivity: Expanding Psychoanalytic Identity for the AI Age.
source: PubMed · Journal of the American Psychoanalytic Association
desc: [Journal of the American Psychoanalytic Association] This article recognizes that the artificial intelligence (AI) age is reconfiguring conditions for intimacy, clinical care, and psychoanalytic professional identity. Beginning with AI-anxiety as a response to transformative change and technological peril, it highlights hope, not as optimism but as an active way of being that permits sustained engagement. Against the reassuring claim that machines can never do what psychoanalysts do, the article distinguishes performance from process: Relational AI may soon replicate expert clinical behavior without replicating human subjectivity, embodiment, or unconscious life. What remains irreducible is the meaning-making context of human care, including the fact that analytic speech acts derive meaning and force from being offered by a vulnerable, invested human other. The article then introduces techno-subjunctivity to describe the new relational field created by anthropomorphic AI: an illusion of intimacy in which users oscillate between feeling recognized by a responsive other while knowing they are interacting with a machine without interiority. Psychoanalytic identity, the article concludes, must expand to include AI-fitness. Such direct experience with AI's relational pull along with critical psychoanalytic reflection will enable clinicians to accompany patients and students through techno-subjunctive life without denial, shame, or surrender.

title: Leveraging artificial intelligence for livestock genetics and breeding.
source: PubMed · Journal of animal science and biotechnology
desc: [Journal of animal science and biotechnology] The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming modern society including animal genetics and breeding which is essential for meeting global nutritional needs in supplying milk, meat, and eggs among the most complete sources of protein and micronutrients. Although animal breeding has a long history of using data-driven prediction methods, the application of modern AI approaches remains at a relatively early stage and shows substantial potential for wide-ranging applications in animal genetics and breeding. This study aims to review the current use of AI tools in livestock species across three major applications of high interest: AI-assisted phenotyping, AI-enabled dissection of complex-trait biology (focusing on AI-assisted GWAS and AI-for-omics), and AI-assisted genomic prediction. In addition, we discussed emerging methods and tools developed in human genetics that are not yet widely adopted in farm animals but may offer translational potential for future livestock studies. Looking ahead, AI breakthroughs in livestock genetics and breeding are likely to be driven by increases in data scale and resolution, enhanced computational capacities, standardized data infrastructure and benchmarking, and systematic method development and validation. From a livestock genetic improvement perspective, the key value of AI will lie in integrating AI-generated inputs, including improved phenotyping and biological insights, into practical breeding decisions through statistical modeling.

title: Deep learning-based self-supervised detection and localization of magnetic resonance imaging anomalies in artificial intelligence-supported radiotherapy workflows.
source: PubMed · Physics and imaging in radiation oncology
desc: [Physics and imaging in radiation oncology] Background and purpose: Artificial intelligence is increasingly integrated into radiotherapy workflows, yet it remains vulnerable to out-of-distribution image data that can introduce unexpected behavior in clinical tasks. Deep learning (DL)-based anomaly detection for pelvic magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) remains limited and transparent evaluation for full automation is lacking. This study aimed to develop two self-supervised anomaly-detection framework variations in radiotherapy for pelvic and brain MRI. Materials and methods: A two-stage self-supervised DL-framework was trained separately for pelvic and brain MRI utilizing three public datasets. The first stage compressed normal image data into discrete representations, and a second stage modeled the representation distribution. Anomaly-evidence was obtained by combining perceptual image differences with token-surprisal scores via negative log-likelihood estimation. Automated detection was evaluated for two anatomical cohorts: pelvis, encompassing both synthetic global anomalies and real clinical anomalies, and brain, comprising clinically annotated anomalies. Performance was assessed using sensitivity, specificity, and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). For each cohort, a subset of normal images was reserved for analysis. Results: Promising exploratory performance across evaluation cohorts was obtained. AUCs were 0.97 (95% CI 0.96-0.99) for synthetic pelvic anomalies, 0.95 (95% CI 0.90-1.00) for clinical pelvic anomalies, and 0.81 (95% CI 0.74-0.87) for brain anomalies. Qualitative heatmap analysis showed spatial agreement between detected anomalies and reference annotations. Conclusions: The framework variations showed promising anomaly detection performance across pelvic and brain MRI, supporting its potential for automated MRI quality control in radiotherapy. Heatmap-based visualization further improved interpretability by spatially localizing detected anomalies.

title: Self-Reported AI Competency and Educational Needs for Integrated AI and Digital Rehabilitation Education Among Occupational Therapy Students: A Cross-Sectional Survey.
desc: [Journal of multidisciplinary healthcare] The growing use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in healthcare calls for occupational therapy education that combines critical appraisal, clinical reasoning, and digital rehabilitation. This study aimed to examine students' interest in AI, perceived AI competency, and needs for integrated AI and digital rehabilitation education, and identified factors associated with educational content needs. An exploratory cross-sectional survey using convenience sampling and five researcher-developed scales without full psychometric validation was conducted among occupational therapy students from three universities. A total of 250 questionnaires were submitted, and 230 complete responses were analyzed. Descriptive statistics, reliability tests, Welch group comparisons, Pearson correlations, and hierarchical multiple regression with sensitivity analyses were used. Mean scores were 3.64±0.77 for AI interest, 3.42±0.67 for self-reported AI competency, 3.93±0.68 for educational content needs, 3.95±0.63 for educational priority, and 3.82±0.64 for instructional method preference. All five domains were positively correlated. Educational priority and instructional method preference showed the strongest correlation (r=0.701). AI interest (β=0.490, p<0.001) and self-reported AI competency (β=0.154, p=0.015) were associated with educational content needs in the conventional regression; the final model explained 34.3% of the variance. The competency association was sensitive to robust inference (HC3 p=0.0504). Students expressed preferences for integrated, practice-oriented education addressing AI use, occupational therapy clinical reasoning, client-appropriate tool selection, assessment, and intervention planning.

title: Tissue-resident memory T cells: central regulators of chronicity and relapse in autoimmune diseases-from mechanistic insights to precision interventions.
desc: [Immunologic research] Tissue-resident memory T cells (TRM), a subset of memory T cells that persist long-term within peripheral tissues without recirculating, play a dual role in adaptive immunity. They serve as the frontline defense against pathogen reinfection, yet accumulating evidence implicates TRM cells as pivotal effectors driving chronicity, tissue-specific damage, and clinical relapse in various autoimmune diseases. This review systematically examines the central role of TRM cells in autoimmunity by dissecting the molecular mechanisms underlying their development, maintenance, and activation. We highlight how specific cytokine networks, alongside metabolic programs and sustain their pathogenic potential. Emphasis is placed on the heterogeneous functions of TRM cells in diseases such as psoriasis/psoriatic arthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, lupus and primary Sjögren's syndrome. Furthermore, we analyze the dysregulation of tissue immune checkpoints through interactions between TRM and regulatory T cells (Treg), which disrupt immune homeostasis. Finally, we critically evaluate current therapeutic strategies targeting TRM cells and propose future precision intervention approaches leveraging immune metabolic reprogramming, nanotechnology, and artificial intelligence to improve disease management and prevent relapse.

title: Artificial intelligence and clinical work: Designing GenAI mentoring to support decision making in cognitive rehabilitation.
desc: [Work (Reading, Mass.)] BackgroundOccupational therapists working in cognitive rehabilitation may face high cognitive demands, and professional isolation. Although AI is used for information retrieval and decision support, its role in supporting reflective clinical reasoning remains insufficiently conceptualized. As scholarly attention shifts from automation toward augmentation of professional judgment, the next step is to understand how AI may support reflective reasoning in complex rehabilitation work.ObjectiveTo examine key challenges in cognitive rehabilitation and explore how these needs may inform a conceptual design for GenAI-mediated mentoring within clinical work.MethodsA qualitative study grounded in Design Thinking methodology was conducted with 30 female occupational therapists (age range 24-64 years, M = 41.26, SD = 10.35) with wide range of clinical experience (less than one year to more than 20 years) from diverse settings. They completed a demographic questionnaire and participated in two Design Thinking workshops (n = 14; n = 16). Seven participants subsequently engaged in follow-up interviews to refine design implications. All sessions were audio-recorded, transcribed, and analyzed thematically.ResultsThe thematic analysis yielded four themes: (A) The Therapist's role (B) Challenging therapist-client interactions, (C) Loneliness of the Therapist (D) Expectations for guidance or support aspects. These findings informed the conceptualization of a GenAI mentoring framework grounded in real-world clinical demands.ConclusionsThe findings support the design of generative AI systems as dialogic, context-sensitive tools intended to strengthen professional judgment, warranting further examination of their integration within real-world clinical workflows.

title: From Generative Molecular Design to Agentic Artificial Intelligence in Drug Discovery.
desc: [ChemMedChem] Over the past decade, artificial intelligence (AI) has increasingly influenced the early stages of drug discovery, which focus primarily on target evaluation and the design or identification of new active small molecules or biologics. Deep neural networks adapted from areas such as natural language processing and computer vision have provided novel opportunities for generative modeling and human-machine interactions. State-of-the-art AI models for generative molecular design have emerged, but remain only little understood so far. Furthermore, new computational systems are being devised rapidly that are expected to significantly transform the drug discovery landscape in the near future. These developments pose challenges to computer-aided drug discovery in various ways. In the following, we discuss these opportunities and challenges, with a focus on molecular design.

title: A Deep Learning-Driven Approach for Musical Instrument Sound Synthesis and Acoustic Optimization.
source: PubMed · Journal of visualized experiments : JoVE
desc: [Journal of visualized experiments : JoVE] This structured narrative review examines deep‑learning‑driven musical instrument timbre synthesis, covering playing‑condition control, acoustic defect diagnosis, structural inverse design, and subjective‑objective quality evaluation. Adopting a structured narrative review method, this work follows the main themes of technical paradigms, application closed loops, supporting resources, evaluation evidence, and industrial constraints. Relevant methods are organized as direct fitting of waveforms or spectrograms to hybrid modeling embedded with physical priors, and further toward interpretable end‑to‑end systems built upon differentiable digital signal processing (DDSP) and differentiable physical modeling. A closed‑loop research framework of "multimodal evidence‑physical constraint‑perceptual evaluation‑human‑in‑the‑loop" is proposed in this paper. The major findings are as follows: pure data‑driven models possess strong representation capability yet suffer from data bias and uncontrolled extrapolation; physical priors can boost sample efficiency and parameter interpretability, whereas their benefits depend on the accuracy of priors and optimization stability; differentiable acoustics provides a unified interface for synthesis, inversion, and design, but still encounters challenges including high‑frequency gradient pathology, multi‑physics coupling, real‑time computation and incomplete perceptual objectives. Future research directions include cross‑cultural musical‑instrument datasets, digital twins with uncertainty estimation, auditable auditory preference models, low‑latency edge‑end deployment, and governance of copyright and performer rights. This study provides a unified conceptual framework and reusable evaluation pathways for music‑acoustics researchers, algorithm developers, and lutherie engineers.

title: Words matter: matching language to biological certainty in assisted reproduction.
source: PubMed · Journal of assisted reproduction and genetics
desc: [Journal of assisted reproduction and genetics] Assisted reproduction depends on concise labels to translate complex gamete and embryo phenotypes into clinically useful information. Yet such labels do not remain purely descriptive. Morphology-based classifications can influence whether an embryo is biopsied, cryopreserved, transferred or discarded; shape patient understanding; define research variables; and become training targets for artificial-intelligence models. The issue is therefore not simply semantic, but how observations acquire inference as they move into decisions, datasets and algorithms. A deviation from an expected phenotype does not necessarily indicate dysfunction, a lower morphological rank does not establish non-viability, and a reference limit is not an individual diagnosis. We argue that terminology in assisted reproduction should be proportional to biological certainty and preserve the distinction between observation, phenotype, ranking, prognosis and demonstrated abnormality. We further propose a pragmatic semantic framework for maintaining those distinctions across clinical communication, research and data-driven applications.

title: Rethinking neural network reparameterized full waveform inversion: A Hessian perspective.
source: PubMed · Neural networks : the official journal of the International Neural Network Society
desc: [Neural networks : the official journal of the International Neural Network Society] By seamlessly integrating deep neural networks (DNNs) into the traditional full waveform inversion (FWI) framework, the neural-network-reparameterized FWI (RFWI) naturally introduces implicit regularization, thereby mitigating key challenges in practical applications-such as sensitivity to initial models and susceptibility to local minima. While a variety of advanced RFWI methods have been proposed to enhance inversion performance, profound insights remain lacking in two key questions: (1) How does the DNN improve the robustness of RFWI, (2) How to further improve the performance of RFWI. In response to the first question, the Hessian spectrum is introduced as an analytical tool to reveal the difference in optimization characteristics between RFWI and traditional FWI. Our findings demonstrate that the superior robustness arises from the persistent constraints imposed by DNN on the inversion process, guiding a long-lasting tendency towards the eigenvectors associated with large eigenvalues, which correspond to stable directions dominated by low-frequency information. For the second question, we propose two improvement techniques based on the inherent optimization characteristics of RFWI, targeting convergence or robustness, both of which have the potential to generalize to other RFWI implementations. Focusing on convergence improvement in ideal scenarios, we propose the Adam+L-BFGS hybrid optimizer, which accelerates high-frequency fitting while avoiding local minima. Regarding robustness improvement in challenging scenarios, we propose a Hessian trace-based regularization technique that promotes flatter optimization trajectories, thereby mitigating the overfitting of noise. The experimental results support the effectiveness of our proposed improvement techniques.
